introduction-shifting-security-left.core: Shifting left means finding security issues as early as possible: in the IDE, on commit, and in CI, rather than in a pre-release pentest or in production. Bugs are cheaper to fix when the author still has context. Different scanners see different things. SAST reads source code, SCA checks dependencies, container scanning checks images, DAST attacks a running app, and runtime protection watches production. A layered pipeline uses each where it is strongest and tunes for low noise so developers keep trusting the results.

first_principles.problem: A critical vulnerability found two days before launch delays the release by a month.
derivation: Scan in **IDE and PRs** (SAST, SCA, secrets).

analogy.title: Checking ingredients before cooking instead of after serving
analogy.story: Spotting a bad egg in the fridge is cheap; finding it after the dinner party isn't.
analogy.breaks: Shift left doesn't remove the need to watch production (shift right).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Issues surface on the PR, while context is fresh.

code.text:
jobs:
  security:
    steps:
      - run: semgrep ci                 # SAST
      - run: gitleaks detect            # secrets
      - run: osv-scanner -r .           # SCA
      - run: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL app:${{ github.sha }}

check.q: Why does noise matter so much in shift-left tooling?
check.a: Developers ignore or bypass tools full of false positives, which defeats the purpose.

sast-the-code-spellchecker.core: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) analyses source code without running it, looking for dangerous patterns and data flows: user input (source) reaching a SQL query or shell call (sink) without sanitisation. Tools range from pattern matchers (Semgrep) to deep dataflow engines (CodeQL). SAST finds bugs early and points to exact lines, but it can't see runtime config and produces false positives, so it needs tuned rules and triage.

first_principles.problem: Code review misses a string-formatted SQL query buried in a helper three calls deep.
truths: Code can be analysed before it runs.
Taint flows from source to sink.

analogy.title: A spellchecker and grammar checker
analogy.story: It underlines suspicious words as you type, without needing anyone to read the document aloud.
analogy.breaks: A spellchecker flags valid jargon; SAST likewise flags safe code (false positives).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Unsafe queries are flagged on the line where they're written.

code.text:
rules:
  - id: sql-fstring
    languages: [python]
    severity: ERROR
    message: SQL built with f-string; use parameters
    pattern: $CUR.execute(f"...")

check.a: Issues depending on runtime config or environment, like a misconfigured server or missing auth at the proxy.

dast-the-simulated-hacker.core: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) attacks a running application from the outside, the way a black-box attacker would: crawling pages and APIs, then sending malicious payloads (XSS, SQLi, header tampering) and observing responses. It finds runtime and configuration issues SAST can't see, and is language-agnostic, but it is slower, needs a deployed environment and auth setup, and can't point to the exact code line.

first_principles.problem: SAST is clean, but a staging deploy exposes a reflected XSS through a reverse-proxy rewrite and missing security headers.
truths: Coverage depends on crawling and auth.
derivation: Feed it **OpenAPI specs** for API coverage.
Run **baseline scans** per deploy, full scans nightly.

analogy.title: A hired burglar testing your house
analogy.story: They don't read the blueprints; they rattle doors and windows and report which ones opened.
analogy.breaks: A burglar explores every room; DAST only tests what it can crawl or is told about.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Runtime issues are caught before production.

code.text:
docker run -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable zap-baseline.py \
  -t https://staging.app.example.com -r zap.html
# API scan from spec
docker run -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable zap-api-scan.py \
  -t https://staging.app.example.com/openapi.json -f openapi

check.a: SAST sees code paths but not runtime; DAST sees runtime but not code. Together they cover each other's gaps.

sca-checking-your-supply-chain.core: Software Composition Analysis (SCA) inventories your open-source dependencies, including transitive ones, and matches them against vulnerability databases (CVE, GHSA, OSV) and licence policies. Most application code is third-party, so a single library (Log4j) can expose thousands of apps. Good SCA produces an SBOM, prioritises by reachability and exploitability (KEV, EPSS) rather than CVSS alone, and automates upgrades with tools like Dependabot or Renovate.

first_principles.problem: Log4Shell lands, and the team can't say which of 200 services include log4j-core, even transitively.
truths: Transitive deps are invisible without tooling.

analogy.title: A food recall check on your pantry
analogy.story: When a supplier recalls a batch, you need to know which tins on your shelves came from it.
analogy.breaks: Tins don't contain other tins; dependencies nest many levels deep.

code.text:
syft dir:. -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json   # inventory
grype sbom:sbom.json --fail-on high        # match vulns
# answer 'are we affected?' in seconds:
jq '.components[] | select(.name=="log4j-core") | .version' sbom.json

points: Dependencies are most of your code.

check.q: Why prioritise by EPSS/KEV rather than CVSS alone?
check.a: CVSS measures severity, not likelihood; KEV and EPSS indicate real-world exploitation.

container-scanning-trivy-and-grype.core: Container scanning inspects image layers for vulnerable OS packages and language libraries, embedded secrets, and misconfigurations (running as root, no USER). Trivy and Grype read package databases inside the image and match them against advisories. Scan at build in CI, again in the registry as new CVEs appear, and at admission in Kubernetes. Minimal base images (distroless, Alpine, Chainguard) remove most findings at the source.

first_principles.problem: An image built on a full Ubuntu base ships with 400 CVEs, mostly in packages the app never uses.
derivation: Scan in **CI**, fail on critical with fixes.

analogy.title: X-raying luggage before it boards
analogy.story: You check the bag at check-in, but also re-screen if a new threat is discovered on the flight list.
analogy.breaks: Luggage doesn't change after screening; image risk changes as new CVEs are published.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Builds fail only on fixable, serious issues.

code.text:
trivy image --ignore-unfixed --severity HIGH,CRITICAL \
  --exit-code 1 registry.example.com/app:1.4.2
trivy config Dockerfile      # e.g. flags missing USER
# FROM gcr.io/distroless/static  → near-zero OS CVEs

check.q: Why use --ignore-unfixed in a CI gate?
check.a: Failing builds on CVEs with no available fix blocks delivery without giving developers an action to take.

runtime-protection-the-security-camera.core: Runtime protection watches workloads while they run, because some attacks only show at runtime: zero-days, stolen credentials, or a compromised dependency doing something new. Tools such as Falco and Tetragon use eBPF to observe syscalls, process launches, file access and network connections, alerting on deviations (a shell spawned in a container, writes to /etc, outbound connections to mining pools) or blocking them. It complements shift-left scanning by covering what can't be known before deployment.

first_principles.problem: A clean, scanned image is exploited through a zero-day, and an attacker opens a reverse shell that nobody notices for weeks.
truths: Not all threats are knowable before deploy.
Kernel-level visibility is hard to evade.
derivation: Define **behaviour rules** (no shells, no unexpected egress).

analogy.title: CCTV in a shop after the door locks are checked
analogy.story: Locks keep most people out; cameras catch whoever gets in anyway.
analogy.breaks: Cameras only record; runtime tools can also stop the action.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The reverse shell triggers an alert within seconds.

code.text:
- rule: Shell in container
  desc: interactive shell spawned in a container
  condition: spawned_process and container and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh)
  output: "shell in %container.name (user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING

check.q: Why is runtime protection needed if images are scanned?
check.a: Scanning finds known flaws; runtime catches exploitation of unknown ones and malicious behaviour.
